The rule is consistent rather than an exception: `--format` ships on `migrate apply/diff/lint/status` and `schema apply/clean/diff/inspect` because CE executes those verbs, so their report payload is measurable; `schema plan` aborts on CE and Atlas publishes help text only, so its payload field names are unknown and a Ptah-shaped payload would fail Pro templates referencing Atlas's. `--directive` is deferred because the measured Atlas `.plan.hcl` artifact (internal/atlasschema/testdata/atlas-plan-oracle/plan.hcl) carries only from/to/migration, so a directive would have to ride inside the migration heredoc in an unmeasured spelling — and Ptah's own Atlas-format reader ignores `-- atlas:checkpoint` today (#954), so emitted directives would be silent no-ops Filed as stokaro/ptah#1700 during the 2026-08-19 gap audit: the deferral was a recorded decision with no owner, which is indistinguishable from an oversight once the reasoning ages. Implemented 2026-08-20 on the first branch of that issue's definition of done, which is why the cell is own rather than yes: the capability is here, and what is out of reach is wire compatibility with a payload only the hosted product emits. `--format` renders through internal/atlasreport the way the other eight verbs do, over a payload whose field names are documented under Reference / Atlas commands and chosen to match the sibling verb - `.Changes[].Cmd` is `schema diff`'s spelling, so a template written there reads a plan unchanged - plus `.Name`, `.Dialect`, `.From`, `.To`, `.Exclude`, `.Destructive` and `.MigrationBody`. It selects the output rather than adding to it: the plan-block preview and the saved-to line are suppressed, a plan asked to be saved is still saved, and a synced schema renders the template rather than a sentence, so the outcome a scripted caller hits most often is still parseable. The shared helper set is registered unguarded, unlike `schema diff` where it sits behind PTAH_SCHEMA_DIFF_TEMPLATE_HELPERS - that guard exists because the pinned community binary offers `sql` alone there, and it runs this verb not at all. `--directive` writes the line into the plan file's migration header, in the leading comment block the Atlas family is read from, and two keys are accepted because two subsystems honor them: atlas:txmode none|file, which `schema apply --plan` resolves against --tx-mode through the same function a versioned migration's directive goes through (the directive wins, and the --tx-mode all combination is refused rather than silently decided), and atlas:nolint, which `schema plan lint` already reads out of the SQL. Everything else is refused, atlas:checkpoint included, because a directive the reviewer approves and the run ignores is the defect stokaro/ptah#954 describes. Directives are left in the migration text rather than lifted into a plan-file field for that same reason: the header is shared, and a layer that claimed it would have had to refuse the lines it does not own. Proven against a live PostgreSQL by integration/atlas_schema_plan_directive_e2e_test.go, whose observable is pg_indexes rather than an exit code: a plan carrying CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY applies and the index exists when the directive supplies the mode, the same plan without it fails and the index is absent, and the operator supplying --tx-mode none by hand reaches the same end state. `validate` and `lint` still refuse --format, and the refusal now names why - they report a verdict on a plan rather than producing one - instead of answering "not yet".

With nothing referencing them, ptah-compat output is read by that binary at exit 0 and round-trips through Ptah at exit 0. `PTAH_ATLAS_INSPECT_ALL_BLOCKS=1` output is byte-identical to Ptah's pre-suppression output; the variable is inert on native `ptah schema inspect` (cmd/atlas/schema_inspect_refused_blocks_internal_test.go, internal/atlashclrender/atlas_refused_blocks_test.go). Control: GIN indexes over jsonb and tsvector resolve to core operator classes, still omit the block, and are read by the pinned binary at exit 0. Only an object the render writes counts: measured 2026-08-08 on the same server, `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv AS SELECT id, n FROM src; CREATE INDEX mv_gin ON mv USING gin (n int4_ops)` inspects to a document with no index block at all (`warning: index mv_gin: index cannot be rendered because the target table is absent from the exported schema`), and keeping btree_gin for it made the pinned binary refuse the whole file with `postgres: extensions are not supported by this version` where the same document without the block is read at exit 0 and both apply at exit 0 (stokaro/ptah#1286). The exemption reads the top level only, on both tools. It used to recurse here, on the ground that Ptah's registrar executed nested files, and that entry documented only the UNHASHED nested shape while saying nothing about the hashed one, which was wide open: measured 2026-08-03 against the pinned Atlas CE v1.3.0, on `1_a.sql` + `sub/2_b.sql` both tools wrote a byte-identical atlas.sum listing ONLY `1_a.sql`, both `migrate validate` exited 0 with empty streams, and then `migrate apply` created table `a` on CE and `a`, `b` AND a `pwned` table appended to the nested file AFTER hashing on ptah-compat — SQL executing that no checksum covered or could cover, at exit 0, on a directory both tools called clean. Exit codes and stdout stay byte-identical; only stderr differs. The same narrowing applies to native `ptah --dir-format atlas`, which had the identical hole (measured: base wrote an atlas.sum covering `1_a.sql` and executed `a` and `b`); native auto mode keeps recursing and stays self-consistent because its ptah.sum is computed FROM discovery and covers `sub/2_b.sql` too. Native verbs do not yet print the declined-file warning. Native `ptah migrations up` deliberately stays permissive on a never-hashed directory and reports `migration sum verification failed: atlas.sum not found; run 'ptah migrations hash --dir-format atlas' to create it` only under --verify-sum (exit 2). Directories read through ?format= (goose/flyway/liquibase/dbmate/golang-migrate) are gated on the atlas.sum the SOURCE directory carries, verified before the source layout is parsed and before the database is opened (stokaro/ptah#973, on top of #984 and #992). Resolved 2026-08-20 by the decision on stokaro/ptah#1625, which removed the attribute rather than implementing it: a refresh is an operation, not schema state. A PostgreSQL-family materialized view is populated by its own CREATE, a changed body is reconciled as a DROP and a CREATE that populates it again, and it goes stale when its SOURCE DATA changes - which schema reconciliation cannot observe, so inferring a refresh from a schema change would put an unbounded data operation into a migration. CONCURRENTLY is an option of the explicit statement, not persistent state, and no catalog records a policy: the PostgreSQL reader had to synthesize `manual` for every view to have something to report, and the comparator then diffed that invention against the declaration. Both sides are gone. The attribute is refused where a declaration is PARSED rather than where a dialect is selected, so it cannot be rescued by --exclude or by a `dialects=` scope, and it is refused on presence before its value is read, so `refresh_strategy` bare, empty, null, a bare HCL identifier and sql(...) all fail the same way; the refusal carries the reason instead of reading as a typo, because the name stays a recognized-but-retired attribute rather than being deleted from the metadata. note: Functions and procedures render, read and plan on the PostgreSQL and MySQL families and SQL Server. ClickHouse and SQLite host neither.
evidence: Measured on live MySQL 26.7.0 and MariaDB 12.3.2 (stokaro/ptah#1461, #1470): a function declared once, applied through the planner and read back out of information_schema.ROUTINES and information_schema.PARAMETERS diffs to nothing, diffs to nothing again after a second apply, and reports exactly one named change when one property is changed. The reader now also records DEFINER and CURRENT_USER(): changing a foreign SQL SECURITY DEFINER routine is refused before SQL planning, leaves the catalog body and owner unchanged, and succeeds when the same owner performs the comparison. Volatility is encoded across IS_DETERMINISTIC and SQL_DATA_ACCESS because those are the only catalog columns that survive the read: of the fifteen combinations of the two axes, six are accepted under the pinned image's binary-logging defaults and only two of those are NOT DETERMINISTIC, so IMMUTABLE, STABLE and VOLATILE take three distinct cells. Routine names compare case-insensitively, which is the engines' rule for routines and not the rule their identifier semantics carry for tables. A `language` other than `sql` is named as skipped rather than refused, because Ptah has no way to scope a declared object to a dialect (stokaro/ptah#1471) and refusing would make one schema applied across postgres, mysql and mariadb impossible. REAL and the NATIONAL character-set spellings are refused: REAL reads back as `double` or `float` depending on whether sql_mode includes REAL_AS_FLOAT, and NATIONAL VARCHAR(10) reports the same DTD_IDENTIFIER as VARCHAR(10), differing only in CHARACTER_SET_NAME. Atlas columns from stokaro/ptah-atlas-conformance PARITY.md: "Atlas CE silently omits Pro-gated objects (views, triggers, functions, sequences) from inspection — no error, exit 0" Corrected 2026-08-19: the previous note read as though only MySQL and MariaDB read functions back. The PostgreSQL reader has read them for longer - name, arguments, identity arguments, result type, language, prosecdef, provolatile, prosrc and comment - and overload identity was settled by #1688. What no reader returns is a procedure: both filter to functions only, and aggregates and window functions are excluded by the same predicate, with no report that a kind was left out. That is stokaro/ptah#1722. Updated 2026-08-20: procedures are modeled, measured live on PostgreSQL 18.4 and MySQL 26.7. Both readers filtered them out with nothing saying so -- `AND p.prokind = 'f'` and `ROUTINE_TYPE = 'FUNCTION'` -- so a database holding one produced a clean diff and the operator was told a whole object kind matched when it had never been looked at. A declaration reaches the server, the read returns it, the comparison is empty, CALL runs it, and a removal is dropped with the verb its object takes. Three measured details forced the shape: PostgreSQL prints a procedure's arguments as `IN n integer` and a function's as `n integer`, so the comparison folds the default mode on both sides and nothing else; `pg_get_function_result` is NULL for a procedure, which is the catalog stating the property the two kinds differ in; and MySQL keys information_schema.PARAMETERS by SPECIFIC_NAME, which one schema can hold twice once both kinds are read, so the parameter map is keyed by kind and name. Aggregates and window functions stay out, and the query now says why: both are defined by naming other routines rather than by a body a schema can carry. A related silent no-op went with it -- `DROP FUNCTION f()` names the zero-argument overload, so a drop of a routine taking arguments removed nothing and, behind IF EXISTS, reported success; the bare name is emitted instead, which PostgreSQL refuses only when it is ambiguous. Closed by stokaro/ptah#1784, which asked first whether the T-SQL routine-header parser stokaro/ptah#1720 built for functions could carry a procedure. It is not needed: measured on SQL Server 2025, sys.parameters reports a procedure's parameters exactly as it reports a function's, so only the body comes out of the statement text. That body needs its own walk -- the function one scans past RETURNS, which a procedure has none of, so it runs off the end and returns the whole CREATE statement -- and the walk has to skip the AS in `WITH EXECUTE AS OWNER`, because a procedure created with that clause keeps both words in sys.sql_modules.definition and taking the first AS reports `OWNER AS BEGIN ... END` as the body. Renderer, reader, planner and capability.SQLServer2022.Procedures landed together, with a live round trip: declared, rendered, applied, read back, and the comparator has nothing left to do. A live run also found the half no offline test would have -- a modified procedure is planned as a drop and a create, and the drop half was built without the kind, so it rendered DROP FUNCTION for a procedure, which the server answers with "does not exist" about an object that is right there. T-SQL differences the renderer carries: a procedure takes its parameters without parentheses, and it has no RETURNS clause.

note: Roles and grants on every engine that has them. Row-level security on the PostgreSQL family, SQL Server and ClickHouse; MySQL, MariaDB and Spanner have no such object to model.
evidence: capability.go: Postgres16, CockroachDB23 and YugabyteDB25 set RoleManagement and RowLevelSecurity true; SQLServer2022 sets RoleManagement true and RowLevelSecurity false; SpannerPostgres clears both. SQL Server joined in stokaro/ptah#1698, measured on 17.0.4075.5: a schema grant needs `ON SCHEMA::[name]` and a bare name resolves as an OBJECT instead, `GRANT USAGE` is `Incorrect syntax near 'USAGE'`, and `CREATE ROLE [r] LOGIN` is `Incorrect syntax near 'LOGIN'` because a database role has none of PostgreSQL's cluster attributes -- so a declaration carrying one is refused rather than warned about, since the reader can only ever report them false and the comparison would otherwise report the same pending change forever. Live round trip: integration/dbschema.TestSQLServerLiveRoleAndGrantRoundTrip. Measured 2026-08-10 with capability-probe against CockroachDB CCL v26.2.5 and YugabyteDB 2026.1.0.0: both lines now report AGREES for role_management and row_level_security, closing issue #1376's false-negative preset rows. Live schema-file coverage still reads CREATE ROLE / GRANT / CREATE POLICY / ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and renders each back (issue #932; internal/schemafile.TestLoadAll_PostgresObjectKindsSurviveSQLSchemaFiles). Measured 2026-08-01, CE v1.2.0 (scratch env): `schema apply` with `role "app" { }` on sqlite -> exit 0 'Schema is synced, no changes to be made' (silent no-op). Atlas pricing page (atlasgo.io/pricing, retrieved 2026-08-01): 'Database Security as Code' is Pro, not Starter. Role reads are scoped to the inspected schemas (issue #1267). Measured 2026-08-08 on PostgreSQL 17.10 in two private containers on their own ports, removed at the end: on a database holding one table and cluster roles nothing grants anything to, `ptah db read` went from 4 CREATE ROLE to 0 and `ptah-compat schema apply -u <cluster B> --to <cluster A> --dry-run` from 3 planned CREATE ROLE to 0. With PTAH_POSTGRES_INSPECT_ALL_ROLES=1 both numbers come back (4 and 3), `--auto-approve` created those three roles in cluster B at exit 0 with the pg_roles catalog asserted, and the next dry-run reported 'Schema is synced, no changes to be made'. Comparison is identical under both settings: an existing out-of-scope role plans nothing, a declared attribute change still plans ALTER ROLE, and a role that exists nowhere still plans CREATE ROLE. What the default leaves out is reported on stderr rather than dropped in silence (internal/rolescope; integration/gonative.TestPostgreSQLUndescribedRolesAreReportedAndRecoverableIntegration, which skips without POSTGRES_TEST_DSN). A flag was not used because the conformance cli-surface tier asserts flag parity with the pinned binary. A scoped description also replays, which is the point of scoping it: measured 2026-08-08 on the same PostgreSQL 17.10 container, `ptah-compat schema inspect -u file://<its own inspect output> --dev-url <clean sibling database in the same cluster>` went from exit 1 at `role "ptah_user" already exists (SQLSTATE 42710)` to exit 0, with the re-rendered document byte-identical to the input (diff exit 0, 1265 bytes). A dev materialization does not re-create a role its server already has -- resetting a database does not clear the server's roles -- and it names the skipped roles on stderr; a role the server lacks is still created there, asserted in pg_roles. The pinned Atlas community binary v1.3.0 reads the same document at exit 0 against its own separate, freshly created dev database, emitting no role block of its own (integration.TestAtlasCompatInspectRoleReplayE2E and TestAtlasCompatInspectCreatesARoleTheServerLacksE2E, which skips without POSTGRES_TEST_DSN). ClickHouse joined the roles-and-grants half on 2026-08-16 (stokaro/ptah#1025) and is deliberately absent from the row-level-security half, because capability.ClickHouse24 leaves RowLevelSecurity false and the engine has no policy object. capability.RoleManagement stopped being documented as PostgreSQL role management in the same change: the key promises that a declared role and grant can be planned, rendered, introspected and compared, not that any particular attribute exists. A ClickHouse role carries none at all — system.roles is (name, id, storage) — so internal/clickhouserbac refuses a declared password, login, superuser, createdb, createrole or replication rather than dropping it, and the renderer refuses ALTER ROLE. Grants are managed at database and table scope only; column-scoped grants, wildcard and global scopes, GRANT ALL, ClickHouse users, role membership, quotas, row policies and settings profiles are outside the capability, and declaring the same privilege on both db.* and db.t is refused because the server absorbs the narrower row and the pair could never converge. Measured live 2026-08-16 against clickhouse-server 26.7.3.19: the full apply, re-apply, grant-option add, grant-option revoke and grant removal round trip converged and left an unmanaged role untouched, with each step observed in system.grants. Ptah does not drop ClickHouse roles, and a managed role carrying a partial revoke fails the comparison rather than comparing equal, because a declaration cannot express a grant with an exception SQL Server's row-level security joined in stokaro/ptah#1699: SQLServer2022 sets RowLevelSecurity true because the renderer emits CREATE/DROP SECURITY POLICY, internal/dbschema/mssql reads sys.security_policies joined to sys.security_predicates, and the shared planner plans them. The key promises convergence rather than portability -- a PostgreSQL policy does not port unchanged, because T-SQL has neither an inline predicate expression nor a role list, and permits one enabled policy per table. The two engines this row names apart were measured rather than assumed, because the row named them without an owner. ClickHouse 26.7.3.19 IS a gap: `CREATE ROW POLICY p ON db.t USING tenant = 1 TO role`, `ALTER ROW POLICY ... USING` and `DROP ROW POLICY IF EXISTS` are all accepted, and system.row_policies returns select_filter, is_restrictive and apply_to_list as columns rather than as a statement, so the read half needs no parser -- filed as stokaro/ptah#1736, where the preset's false carried no recorded reason at all. Spanner is NOT a gap: on the PGAdapter emulator v0.55.2 `CREATE ROLE` and `GRANT` answer `Statement is not supported`, pg_roles does not exist, and `ALTER TABLE ... ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` answers `Operation is not supported in <ALTER TABLE> statement`. ClickHouse's row policies landed in stokaro/ptah#1736: the renderer emits CREATE and ALTER ROW POLICY, the reader takes system.row_policies back into DBSchema.RLSPolicies behind the same access-denied degradation the RBAC read uses, and the planner plans them. Three measured facts shape it. A replacement is ALTER, not CREATE: `CREATE OR REPLACE ROW POLICY` is a syntax error and `CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS` against an existing policy succeeds while changing nothing, which the live round trip caught. `WITH CHECK` parses and is then discarded, so a declaration carrying one is named rather than applied with reads filtered and writes open. And `FOR ALL` and `FOR SELECT` are stored identically -- SHOW CREATE ROW POLICY reports a policy created FOR ALL back as FOR SELECT -- so an explicitly declared SELECT cannot converge and is named instead. MySQL and MariaDB joined the role column in stokaro/ptah#1762. Corrected 2026-08-20: the note said row-level security reached everyone but ClickHouse, and both halves were wrong. Measured with a binary built from master: `schema render --dialect clickhouse` over a declared policy emits `CREATE ROW POLICY IF NOT EXISTS ... AS PERMISSIVE FOR SELECT USING ... TO reader`, which stokaro/ptah#1736 landed and closed; the same declaration on mysql and mariadb is named as a skip, because those engines have no row-level security feature at all rather than because Ptah declines to model one. capability.RowLevelSecurity is true for the PostgreSQL family, ClickHouse and SQL Server, and false for MySQL, MariaDB and Spanner, which is the same split.

feature: Domains, composite types, and range types
note: Domains and composites compare and change in place, each kind gated per target. Range types rebuild because PostgreSQL offers no ALTER TYPE ... AS RANGE.
evidence: Measured 2026-08-08 on a binary built from this branch: `ptah schema render` over a domain/composite/range fixture emits all three for postgres, cockroachdb, yugabytedb and spanner alike (the render-side omission issue #929 items 1 and 4 reported was closed by #1221). A changed range subtype used to produce an empty plan while `schema apply` reported "Schema is synced, no changes to be made." over a database still holding the old definition; the reader now introspects subtype_opclass, collation, canonical and subtype_diff, the comparator reports RangesModified and the planner recreates the type, verified converging on live PostgreSQL 17.10 (#931 item 2). Measured 2026-08-03, pinned community binary (reports "atlas community version v1.3.0") vs ptah-compat built from this branch, against PostgreSQL 16 in Docker. Fixture schema "kinds" holds CREATE DOMAIN us_postal, CREATE TYPE addr AS (city text, zip text), CREATE TYPE int_span AS RANGE, a sequence and pg_trgm. `atlas schema inspect --url <pg> -s kinds` returns exactly `table "anchor"` plus `schema "kinds"`; ptah-compat on the same URL returns domain, composite, range, sequence and extension blocks. In the writing direction a domain or composite block in a schema file leaves the community binary printing "Schemas are synced, no changes to be made." - dropped in silence, not refused. Atlas features page (atlasgo.io/features), retrieved 2026-08-03: `Domain types`, `Composite types` and `Range types` are each listed under the PostgreSQL Pro Plan features. Same control as the extensions row. Corrected 2026-08-19. domainChanges compares base type and NOT NULL only, so a changed CHECK or DEFAULT produces no diff and no diagnostic; domains and composites take the drop-and-recreate path the note attributed to range types alone, which is the honest case because PostgreSQL has no ALTER TYPE ... AS RANGE; and because the three kinds have no capability key, VisitCreateType emits CREATE DOMAIN for CockroachDB, which refuses it at apply time rather than being told before SQL. Tracked by stokaro/ptah#1717. Updated 2026-08-19: measured on live PostgreSQL 18.4. The comparison no longer declines CHECK and DEFAULT. The declaration is put through the same rewrite the catalog form already made -- a domain over the declared base type is created in the session's temporary schema inside a transaction that is rolled back, and its stored expressions are read back -- so `VALUE IN ('a','b')` compares against `(VALUE = ANY (ARRAY['a'::text, 'b'::text]))` as like with like. A domain unchanged since it was created reports no difference; a changed CHECK reports one, where before it produced neither diff nor diagnostic and `schema apply` called the schema synced over a database still enforcing the old rule. The change is then applied with ALTER DOMAIN DROP CONSTRAINT / ADD CHECK rather than by rebuilding: with the drop-and-recreate path restored as a mutant, the same plan fails on a table using the domain with `cannot drop type ... because other objects depend on it (SQLSTATE 2BP01)`, which is why every domain in use was previously unreachable. SET/DROP DEFAULT and SET/DROP NOT NULL take the same route, a base-type change still rebuilds because PostgreSQL has no ALTER DOMAIN ... TYPE, and every ALTER decides against capability.DomainTypes, so a CockroachDB target names the skip. What remains open in stokaro/ptah#1717 is the composite half: ALTER TYPE ADD/DROP ATTRIBUTE exists and is not used yet. Updated 2026-08-19 (composites): ALTER TYPE ADD ATTRIBUTE and DROP ATTRIBUTE replace the rebuild where they reach the declared shape, measured on live PostgreSQL 18.4 against a table whose column has the type -- the case the rebuild cannot serve, because DROP TYPE is refused there. The delta is used only when dropping the removed fields and appending the added ones lands exactly on the declaration: PostgreSQL appends, so a field the declaration puts in the middle is unreachable by ALTER and the comparator falls back to the rebuild rather than planning a change the next comparison would ask for again. A field whose TYPE changed falls back too, because ALTER TYPE ... ALTER ATTRIBUTE is refused on a type in use with CASCADE and without: `cannot alter type "addr" because column "uses_addr.a" uses it`. With the rebuild restored as a mutant the live plan fails on exactly that error; with the ordering simulation removed, the middle-insert fixture reports a delta it cannot reach. Every ALTER decides against capability.CompositeTypes, so a Spanner target names the skip. Range types keep the rebuild and there is no ALTER TYPE ... AS RANGE to replace it with.

Clean on both in that schema scope: empty schema, a lone empty atlas_schema_revisions, a view, a sequence, sqlite_sequence, an empty non-default schema, and a table in another schema. The gate is an adoption gate — once any revision row exists it never fires again, measured on a managed database that grew an unmanaged table and then applied a new migration at exit 0 on both tools. --allow-dirty and --baseline each opt out; passing both exits 1 with 'sql/migrate: baseline and allow-dirty are mutually exclusive' on both tools, which ptah-compat previously accepted at exit 0. The discriminating fixture for the predicate is `--revisions-schema revs`, which leaves `public` holding exactly one table: both tools still refuse and name that table, which rules out 'more than one table' and pins the rule at 'any table other than this run's revision table'. Realm scope was measured separately for stokaro/ptah#1257 on 2026-08-07, PostgreSQL 17, one throwaway database per cell: through a plain postgres:// URL with no search_path the binary evaluates the whole realm and refuses on SCHEMAS. An EMPTY extra schema exits 1 with 'found schema "extra"', a table living only in another schema does the same, and a table in public reports 'found schema "public"' rather than naming the table -- all three of which ptah-compat applied at exit 0 before this change. Tolerated at that scope: an empty public, a view, a sequence, a materialized view, an enum type, a function, an extension, and the run's own revisions schema holding nothing but the revision table. The offender reported is the first by BYTE order ('Zed' before 'app'), and a revisions schema holding more reports a count instead: 'found 2 tables in schema "atlas_schema_revisions"'.
